newsitem.title: UK: Oil price stages mild recovery after early fall.
newsitem.headline: Oil price stages mild recovery after early fall.

text.p: Oil prices staged a half-hearted afternoon recovery on Thursday, clawing back some of the ground lost earlier in the day before drifting back in sight of the day's lows.
After shedding more than $1 a barrel in value over the past two days, rumours of unexpected refinery shutdowns in the United States were enough to draw out fresh buying.

The knee-jerk reaction to even whispers of production problems underlines the oil market's anxiety over supplies at a time of historically low heating oil stocks heading into the peak winter demand period.
"The market is vulnerable to supply shortfalls more than ever," a London trader said.
London December futures for international benchmark Brent crude hit an intraday low of $23.65 a barrel on Thursday, 42 cents down on the day.
The contract drifted higher to $23.96 in late afternoon trade before weakening again to $23.76 at the close, just 11 cents off the day's low.
Traders said they were not surprised at the strength of the fall given the ferocity of the rally which has taken crude oil and heating oil prices to their highest levels since the 1991 Gulf War.

"We had a very good spell at the top and the market needed to let off some steam. After this we can refocus on fundamentals," said Bo Van Wijk, vice-president, energy risk management at Swiss bank UBS in Zurich.
Those same fundamentals which took Brent to a post-Gulf War high of $25.06 last week have not changed, he said.

Oil prices have added $9 since mid-June on a bullish cocktail of political tensions in the oil-rich Middle East and Russia, robust demand and fears that heating oil stocks are too low to meet winter demand.
"Those underlying bullish fundamentals have not disappeared. It is just that the market has another flag up the pole right now," said Mari Buglass, senior energy analyst at Smith, Barney in London.

Traders said hedge funds sitting on long (overbought) positions chose this week to take profits especially after weekly data showed that U.S. heating oil inventories in the key Northeast rose last week.
Inventory data released by the American Petroleum Institute (API) late on Tuesday showed heating oil stocks in the U.S. northeast, the world's largest market, grew by 1.2 million barrels last week.

After a meeting with U.S. Energy Department officials last week, two U.S. refiners said they would maximise distillate output, and late on Monday Colonial Pipeline said it was opening its gasoline line from the Gulf of Mexico to the northeast to distillate shipments for at least 40 days.
But brokers said the market should hold current ranges until there was a better idea what the winter would bring.
Memories of last winter's frigid temperatures have made traders wary of selling short.
"No one will dare try to second-guess what the weather will bring. Normally the cold weather does not hit until January or February," a broker said.
With API data showing heating oil stocks are still 14.8 million barrels below last year's levels, brokers were wary of predicting the end of the rally.
"You really cannot afford to be caught short this early in the season. This is a temporary blip in a very strong market," UBS' Van Wijk said.
